stem: Two hypothetical variants are studied. Variant X produces a shortened protein ending at a newly introduced stop signal. Variant Y produces a full-length protein with one changed amino acid. Both proteins have reduced activity in the same assay. Which of the following best explains why the variants receive different sequence classifications?

options.label: A
options.text: X replaces an amino acid; Y terminates translation early
options.explanation: This reverses the observations. X is shortened at a new stop, whereas Y retains its length and contains an amino-acid substitution in the protein.
options.misconception: Reverses which variant creates a stop signal and which substitutes an amino acid.

options.label: B
options.text: X and Y terminate translation at an earlier stop signal
options.explanation: Only X is reported to end at a new stop. Y remains full length, so its reduced activity should not be attributed to premature termination.
options.misconception: Attributes both activity defects to premature termination even though one protein remains full length.

options.label: C
options.text: X and Y replace a residue without changing protein length
options.explanation: X is explicitly shortened, so a preserved-length substitution cannot explain its result. Y alone has the stated full-length protein with one altered amino acid.
options.misconception: Treats both changes as full-length substitutions despite the measured truncation of one protein.

options.label: D
options.text: X and Y shift the reading frame through a base deletion
options.explanation: Neither result reports a nontriplet deletion. Inferring a frameshift from reduced activity alone ignores the distinct sequence consequences that the experiment directly measured.
options.misconception: Infers a frameshift from reduced activity without evidence of a frame-changing insertion or deletion.

options.label: E
options.text: X terminates translation early; Y replaces an amino acid
options.explanation: Premature termination classifies X as nonsense, while residue substitution classifies Y as missense. Their shared reduction in measured activity does not erase that sequence-level distinction.
options.misconception: No misconception: Different sequence consequences remain distinct even when both variants reduce activity.

context: Learning objective: use the sequence consequence to classify a mutation, then assess function separately. Similar activity measurements can result from different changes in protein sequence and length.
